parsed.explanation: Combined regime is split: the division is among the most protective on paper—statewide gender-identity anti-discrimination in public accommodations, hate-crime enhancements, panic-defense repeal, accessible X markers, and a 2023 shield law for care banned at home. Those protections materially lower everyday risk for an adult visitor once inside. But the national entry and custody layer is not displaced: binary passport/visa rules, discontinued X issuance, secondary screening for discrepancies, refusal and possible lifetime fraud findings, and documented abuse in federal immigration/corrections custody (forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse, conversion practices). A trans visitor is therefore exposed at the border before state law operates. Minors face added national care/school hostility, partly mitigated by the state shield. Enforcement data for accommodations and police are absent. Overall: strong in-state, severe federal chokepoint.

entry_documents.exposure: National binary sex definition; X issuance stopped; existing X valid only until expiry; passports reported confiscated or blocked; discrepancy can trigger refusal and possible lifetime fraud finding.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiration; legal-aid FAQ; national policy remains under court challenge.
entry_documents.interaction: State X markers and anti-discrimination law do not govern federal passport or visa adjudication or border screening.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal immigration custody documented forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement, sexual abuse; federal corrections conversion practices, hormone removal, care denial.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border discrepancy can move the traveller into federal detention before state protections operate.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; federal facilities follow national rules.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no facility ban; statewide public-accommodation law covers gender identity; hate-crime law applies.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State-protected venues and facilities are safer, but federal buildings and funding remain under national rule.

care_services.exposure: National executive orders frame minor care as mutilation; proposed insurance bar; federal investigations; immigration custody care denial.
care_services.protection: 2023 state shield law protects patients and providers for care legal locally but banned at home; state coverage and anti-discrimination.
care_services.interaction: Shield helps in-state care, but federal rules, prosecution and custody care remain outside it.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy lists 'radically pro-transgender' groups as priority; DOJ memo invokes 'radical gender ideology'; official hostility.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State hate-crime enhancement, anti-discrimination, panic-defense repeal; federal hate-crime statute exists.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State law enforcement is likely more protective, but federal task forces and prosecutorial framing can override local climate.

minors_guardians.exposure: National orders target minor transition, school support and care; no documented minor-specific visitor rule beyond documents and care rhetoric.
minors_guardians.protection: State shield law, conversion-therapy ban, anti-bullying and public-accommodation protections.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting trans minor is not in local schools, but federal border, custody and care-investigation threats persist; state shield partly mitigates.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific data on police stops, searches, violence or accommodation enforcement; national climate hostile.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Statewide gender-identity hate-crime enhancement, panic-defense abolition, anti-discrimination; no documented state targeting.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Recourse exists on paper, but charging and prosecution data are absent, so practical protection is uncertain.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: National measures partly enjoined or in litigation; shield-law scope narrowed; accommodation enforcement undocumented; fraud findings discretionary.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Courts have blocked some national orders; state law and legal-aid FAQ provide routes.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Traveller exposure varies with which national measures are operative at entry and whether local remedies are used.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A ends in denial or stranding with invasive review but no imprisonment. This dossier has a comparable border-denial pathway plus documented federal detention abuse, but also a strong state protective regime. The federal chokepoint is worse; the in-state layer is much better, leaving it somewhat above 0.35 but still constrained.

0.55-B shows delay then a functioning transit protection and no detention. Here in-state protections are stronger—accommodation, hate crime, care shield—but the national border and custody layer can refuse entry or detain with documented harm, so it sits below 0.55.

0.75-B has a working hotel non-discrimination code and no federal custody exposure. This jurisdiction matches or exceeds that local protection but adds a hostile national entry and detention regime, so it is materially lower than 0.75.

parsed.synthesis: The operative journey begins with national border and document screening, where a mismatch can trigger invasive review, refusal, fraud consideration, or federal detention; state anti-discrimination and shield laws do not reach that stage. Inside the division, public-accommodation protections, hate-crime penalties, panic-defense repeal and care-shield provisions make hotels, services, care and daily bureaucracy comparatively safe, though enforcement is undocumented. Federal facilities and custody remain a separate hostile system. For a family with a trans minor, state care protections and anti-bullying rules help, but national rhetoric, care restrictions and investigative threats create uncertainty. The rating sits in Elevated Risk: robust local protection cannot cancel the unavoidable federal entry and custody exposure.
